purpose: machine-facing subdomain knowledge base of concrete work units for designing, deploying, and operating a Python-centric backend/API on a Linux server, covering web frameworks, the data layer, Linux operation, containers, scaling, and ops, for use as a node in a knowledge-searcher meta-KB.
assumptions: target is an application backend exposing an HTTP/REST API on a Linux server
Python-centric stack (FastAPI/Flask/Django) with a relational database
no observed dataset, benchmark, or expert-judgment input was supplied; all values are heuristic priors
single-team operation scale rather than large multi-region distributed systems
exclusions: deep distributed-systems theory (consensus, CRDTs) beyond practical scaling

competency_questions.question: Which resources, routes, and versioning rules define the backend API contract clients depend on?
How does a request flow through routing, middleware, and dependencies to a handler and back to a response?
How is request and response data validated, coerced, and serialized so only well-formed data crosses the boundary?
How are callers authenticated and authorized, and where do auth secrets come from?
How is the relational data model designed and accessed through the ORM/query layer?
How is data-layer read/write performance kept acceptable as data grows (indexing, caching, pooling)?
How are schema changes applied safely and reversibly across environments?
How is slow or deferrable work moved off the request path reliably?
How is the backend run and fronted as a managed Linux service behind a reverse proxy?
How is server access and the filesystem secured (SSH, users, permissions)?
How are configuration and secrets managed outside code and per environment?
How is the backend packaged into images and released with migrations and rollback?
How is the backend scaled horizontally behind a load balancer while staying stateless?
How is the running system observed, how do signals drive incident response, and how is the system protected against data loss and recovered after an incident?

glossary.definition: the ordered path a request takes through routing, middleware, and dependencies to a handler and back to a response
object-relational mapper that maps database rows to application objects and builds queries
a versioned, ordered change to the database schema that can be applied and rolled back
a database structure that speeds lookups on chosen columns at the cost of extra write and storage
a managed set of reused database connections shared across requests
a fast secondary store of derived/hot data fronting the source of truth, governed by TTL and invalidation
a broker-backed mechanism that hands deferrable work to background workers with retries
a declarative definition that supervises a process as a Linux service with restart and limits
a server in front of the app that terminates TLS and routes/limits client traffic to upstreams
a sensitive config value (password, key, token) that must stay out of code and logs
the property that internal state can be inferred from logs, metrics, and traces emitted by the system

evidence_label_policy.note: No observed/experimental inputs supplied; only heuristic labels are eligible.

source_registry.description: Heuristic priors from established backend/distributed-systems and Linux engineering literature and practice (Percival & Gregory, Architecture Patterns with Python; Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications; Kerrisk, The Linux Programming Interface) plus framework/ops conventions (FastAPI/Flask/Django, SQL/ORM, nginx, systemd, Docker); no measured dataset supplied.
does_not_support: measured incident or restore success rates
grounding_limits: all numeric values are heuristic priors, not measurements
no observed or experimentally_validated labels are eligible

normalization_definitions.rounding: round computed scores to 2 decimals; tolerance 0.02

nodes.definition: Design the backend's HTTP/REST API surface: resources, routes, verbs, status codes, versioning, and the request/response contract clients depend on.
contradictors: team that exposes leaky ad-hoc endpoints per feature

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when feature scope, client needs, or resource model changes

pros.claim: a stable contract lets clients, data layer, and frontend integrate without churn
pros.example: versioning a /v2 resource instead of mutating /v1 fields

cons.claim: over-designing the contract early slows delivery before requirements settle
cons.example: building HATEOAS for an internal app that never needs it

failure_modes: unversioned breaking change strands clients
verbs/status codes used inconsistently
acceptance_tests: every endpoint has a documented request/response schema
breaking changes are gated behind a new version
revisit_triggers: new resource or breaking field change

nodes.definition: Implement the request/response lifecycle in the web framework: routing, middleware ordering, ASGI/WSGI handling, dependency injection, and exception-to-response mapping.
contradictors: team that puts auth/validation logic in every handler by copy-paste

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the framework, concurrency model, or middleware stack changes

pros.claim: centralizing cross-cutting concerns in middleware removes per-handler duplication
pros.example: one auth dependency injected into every protected route

cons.claim: misunderstanding async vs sync blocks the event loop under load
cons.example: calling a sync DB driver inside an async handler

failure_modes: middleware ordered wrong (auth after handler runs)
blocking call stalls an async event loop

nodes.definition: Validate, coerce, and serialize request and response data with typed schemas so only well-formed data reaches business logic and only safe data leaves.
contradictors: team that trusts client JSON and passes raw dicts downstream

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the API contract or entity schema changes

pros.claim: typed validation at the edge stops malformed data from corrupting downstream logic
pros.example: rejecting a negative quantity before it reaches the order service

cons.claim: duplicating validation in models and handlers drifts out of sync
cons.example: two places define the email regex differently

failure_modes: allow-by-default validation lets extra/unsafe fields through
over-eager serialization leaks internal fields

nodes.definition: Establish who a caller is (authentication) and what they may do (authorization) using sessions, tokens (JWT/OAuth), and access-control rules enforced server-side.
contradictors: team that checks auth only in the UI

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the identity model, roles, or token strategy changes

pros.claim: server-side enforced auth is the gate protecting every other resource
pros.example: denying access to another user's order by ownership check

cons.claim: rolling custom auth instead of vetted libraries invites subtle flaws
cons.example: hand-built JWT verification that forgets to check expiry

failure_modes: missing object-level check enables IDOR
unsigned/none-alg token accepted
sessions never expire
acceptance_tests: every protected route enforces authentication
object-level authorization prevents cross-tenant access
tokens expire and can be revoked

nodes.definition: Design the relational data model: entities, relationships, keys, normalization level, and constraints that keep stored data correct and queryable.
contradictors: team that stores everything as JSON blobs to avoid modeling

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when access patterns, entities, or consistency needs change

pros.claim: a correct schema with constraints prevents whole classes of data corruption
pros.example: a unique constraint stopping duplicate user emails

cons.claim: premature denormalization creates update anomalies
cons.example: copying a price into orders and forgetting to update it

failure_modes: under-modeled schema forces painful later migrations
missing constraints allow inconsistent rows
acceptance_tests: key relationships have enforced foreign-key constraints
schema supports the primary read/write access patterns

nodes.definition: Use the ORM/query layer to read and write data efficiently: mapping, query construction, eager vs lazy loading, transactions, and avoiding N+1 patterns.
contradictors: team that loops queries in application code instead of joining

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the data schema or dominant access patterns change

pros.claim: a disciplined query layer keeps reads efficient and writes transactionally safe
pros.example: eager-loading related rows to render a list in one query

cons.claim: ORM abstraction hides expensive queries until they hit production
cons.example: a lazy attribute access firing a query per row in a loop

failure_modes: N+1 queries explode under list endpoints
unbounded transaction holds locks too long

nodes.definition: Evolve the database schema safely over time with versioned, reversible migrations applied in a controlled order across environments.
contradictors: team that edits production schema by hand

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when a schema change must be applied across environments

pros.claim: versioned reversible migrations make schema change safe and repeatable across environments
pros.example: an additive column migration that rolls back cleanly

cons.claim: a migration that locks a hot table can cause an outage
cons.example: an ALTER on a huge table blocking all writes for minutes

failure_modes: irreversible migration drops data with no recovery
long lock blocks writes during deploy
acceptance_tests: each migration has a tested rollback or forward-fix
a locking migration on a large table is run online or in a window

nodes.definition: Tune database read/write performance through indexes, query plans, and access-pattern-driven optimization so queries stay fast as data grows.
contradictors: team that adds indexes blindly on every column

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when query workload or data volume materially changes

pros.claim: the right indexes turn slow scans into fast lookups on hot paths
pros.example: a composite index matching a frequent WHERE+ORDER BY

cons.claim: every index adds write cost and can be wrong for the real workload
cons.example: indexing a column never used in a predicate

failure_modes: missing index forces full scans at scale
over-indexing slows writes and bloats storage

nodes.definition: Manage database (and other backend) connections with a pool sized and configured so the app uses connections efficiently without exhausting the database.
contradictors: team that opens a new connection per request

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when worker count, DB limits, or load profile change

pros.claim: a correctly sized pool sustains throughput without overwhelming the database
pros.example: sizing workers*pool below the Postgres max_connections

cons.claim: pool math interacts with worker count in non-obvious ways
cons.example: 8 workers x 20 pool exceeding a 100-connection DB limit

failure_modes: pool too small serializes requests under load
pool larger than DB limit exhausts the database

nodes.definition: Add a caching layer (e.g., Redis/in-process) to serve hot reads cheaply, with explicit policies for keys, TTLs, and invalidation to avoid staleness.
contradictors: team that caches everything and never invalidates

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when read hotspots or consistency tolerance change

pros.claim: caching hot reads cuts database load and latency dramatically
pros.example: caching a rarely changing config lookup for 5 minutes

cons.claim: a wrong invalidation rule serves stale data that looks like a bug
cons.example: showing an old price after an update because the key wasn't cleared

failure_modes: missing invalidation serves stale data
cache stampede on expiry hammers the database

nodes.definition: Move slow or deferrable work off the request path into background workers via a task queue, with retries, idempotency, and dead-letter handling.
contradictors: team that runs long work inside the HTTP request

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when workloads, broker, or delivery guarantees change

pros.claim: offloading slow work keeps request latency low and the API responsive
pros.example: sending email and resizing images in a worker instead of the request

cons.claim: at-least-once delivery means tasks can run twice without idempotency
cons.example: charging a card twice because the retry wasn't guarded

failure_modes: non-idempotent task double-runs on retry
unbounded retries flood the broker

nodes.definition: Run the backend as a managed Linux service under systemd with defined start/stop, restart policy, resource limits, logging, and boot ordering.
contradictors: team that runs the app in a screen session by hand

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the host, init system, or service policy changes

pros.claim: systemd gives supervised, repeatable service lifecycle and auto-restart
pros.example: a unit that restarts the API on failure and starts it at boot

cons.claim: a hand-run process dies on disconnect or reboot with no recovery
cons.example: an app launched in a terminal that stops when SSH closes

failure_modes: no restart policy leaves the app down after a crash
missing boot ordering starts the app before the DB is ready
acceptance_tests: the service restarts automatically on crash and on boot
resource limits prevent the service from starving the host

nodes.definition: Place a reverse proxy (nginx) in front of the app for TLS termination, routing, timeouts, buffering, and static/edge concerns between clients and the backend.
contradictors: team that exposes the app server directly to the internet

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when TLS, routing, or edge requirements change

pros.claim: a reverse proxy centralizes TLS, routing, and limits in front of the app
pros.example: terminating HTTPS at nginx and proxying plain HTTP to the app

cons.claim: proxy buffering and header rules can silently break large or streaming responses
cons.example: a low proxy_read_timeout aborting a long export

failure_modes: misconfigured timeouts cut off slow legitimate requests
weak TLS config exposes traffic

nodes.definition: Secure server access and the filesystem: key-based SSH, least-privilege users, and correct file/directory permissions and ownership for app and data paths.
contradictors: team that SSHes as root with password auth

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when operators, hosts, or access policy change

pros.claim: least-privilege access and correct permissions limit blast radius of any compromise
pros.example: running the app as a non-root user with no shell

cons.claim: a single wrong chmod can expose secrets or break the service
cons.example: a 0777 on an env file readable by every account

failure_modes: world-readable secret file leaks credentials
root password SSH enables brute-force takeover
acceptance_tests: password SSH is disabled and key-based auth enforced
app and secret files are not world-readable

nodes.definition: Manage configuration and secrets (DB URLs, API keys, tokens) outside code via environment/secret stores, separated per environment and never committed.

included: keeping secrets out of code and logs

contradictors: team that hardcodes the DB password in the repo

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when secrets, environments, or rotation policy change

pros.claim: externalized, rotatable secrets prevent leaks and ease environment promotion
pros.example: loading the DB URL from an env var injected by the secret store

cons.claim: a leaked secret in code or logs is hard to fully revoke
cons.example: an API key printed in a stack trace shipped to logs

failure_modes: committed secret leaks via git history
secret logged in plaintext during error handling
acceptance_tests: no secret is committed to the repository or printed in logs
secrets differ per environment and can be rotated

nodes.definition: Package the backend and its dependencies into reproducible container images (Docker) with deterministic builds, small surface, and runtime configuration.
contradictors: team that builds images with unpinned latest tags

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when dependencies, base image, or runtime requirements change

pros.claim: reproducible images make deploys consistent across environments
pros.example: pinning the base image and dependencies so a rebuild is identical

cons.claim: bloated or root-running images increase attack surface and pull time
cons.example: a multi-GB image running as root with build tools left in

failure_modes: unpinned base image makes builds non-reproducible
secrets baked into image layers leak

nodes.definition: Release new versions to the server reliably: build, ship, run database migrations, switch traffic, and roll back on failure with minimal downtime.
contradictors: team that copies files to prod and restarts manually

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when release process, migrations, or environments change

pros.claim: a repeatable release with rollback turns deploys from risky events into routine ones
pros.example: blue-green switch that reverts instantly if health checks fail

cons.claim: coupling code and migration order wrong causes mid-deploy breakage
cons.example: new code expecting a column the migration hasn't added yet

failure_modes: code deployed before its migration breaks at runtime
no rollback path turns a bad release into an outage
acceptance_tests: a failed release can be rolled back without data loss
migrations and code deploy in a compatible order

nodes.definition: Scale the backend horizontally behind a load balancer by keeping the app stateless and distributing traffic across multiple workers/instances.
contradictors: team that pins users to one server with in-memory sessions

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when traffic, bottlenecks, or instance topology change

pros.claim: stateless instances behind a load balancer scale horizontally with traffic
pros.example: moving sessions to Redis so any instance can serve any user

cons.claim: adding app instances does nothing if the database is the bottleneck
cons.example: quadrupling workers while a single DB saturates

failure_modes: in-memory session state breaks under multiple instances
scaling app tier just shifts the bottleneck to the database

nodes.definition: Make the running system visible through structured logs, metrics, traces, health checks, and alerts so problems are detected and diagnosed quickly.
contradictors: team that debugs prod with print statements and no metrics

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when critical paths, SLOs, or failure modes change

pros.claim: observability turns opaque failures into diagnosable signals and fast detection
pros.example: an alert firing on error-rate spike before customers notice

cons.claim: logging without structure or correlation makes incident triage slow
cons.example: plain-text logs with no request id across services

failure_modes: no metrics means outages are detected by users first
alert fatigue from noisy thresholds hides real incidents

nodes.definition: Protect against data loss and downtime with tested backups, restore procedures, redundancy, and basic disaster-recovery so the system can recover.
contradictors: team that has backups it has never tried to restore

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when datastores, volumes, or recovery objectives change

pros.claim: tested backups and a restore runbook make data loss recoverable instead of fatal
pros.example: a quarterly restore drill proving the backup actually works

cons.claim: a backup that has never been restored is an unproven assumption
cons.example: discovering during an outage that the dumps were empty

failure_modes: untested backups fail exactly when needed
retention too short to recover from late-discovered corruption
acceptance_tests: a backup can be restored to a working state within the RTO
backups are verified, not just produced

nodes.definition: Operate the system day-to-day and during incidents with runbooks, on-call response, escalation, and postmortems that feed fixes back into the system.
contradictors: team with no runbook that improvises every outage

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when failure modes, on-call structure, or procedures change

pros.claim: runbooks and postmortems turn incidents into faster recovery and durable fixes
pros.example: a documented restart-and-failover runbook executed in minutes

cons.claim: runbooks rot if they are not exercised and updated after incidents
cons.example: a runbook referencing a server that was decommissioned

failure_modes: no runbook makes every incident a slow improvisation
postmortems without follow-through repeat the same outage
acceptance_tests: common failures have a runbook with concrete steps
incidents produce postmortems that close the loop with fixes

edges.why_related: the contract defines the routes and shapes the lifecycle dispatches
edges.benefit_of_coupling: handlers wire to a known route set
edges.risk_of_conflict: building lifecycle before the contract churns routing
edges.example: routing built before endpoints are decided
edges.resolution_rule: define the API contract before wiring the lifecycle

edges.why_related: request/response schemas derive from the contract
edges.risk_of_conflict: validating an undefined contract drifts
edges.example: schemas authored before the contract exists
edges.resolution_rule: fix the contract before authoring validation models

edges.why_related: access patterns in the contract inform the data model
edges.benefit_of_coupling: model serves the real read/write paths
edges.risk_of_conflict: modeling without access patterns mismatches the API
edges.example: schema designed with no view of API needs
edges.resolution_rule: let contract access patterns inform the schema

edges.why_related: validation runs inside the request lifecycle
edges.benefit_of_coupling: validation is a lifecycle stage, not per-handler
edges.risk_of_conflict: validating outside the lifecycle duplicates logic
edges.example: ad-hoc validation in each handler
edges.resolution_rule: place validation in the lifecycle/dependency layer

edges.why_related: auth is enforced as lifecycle middleware/dependencies
edges.benefit_of_coupling: auth applies uniformly to protected routes
edges.risk_of_conflict: auth bolted on per-handler leaves gaps
edges.example: one route forgets its auth check
edges.resolution_rule: enforce auth in the lifecycle, not per handler

edges.why_related: auth needs signing keys/secrets from config
edges.benefit_of_coupling: tokens and sessions use managed secrets
edges.risk_of_conflict: hardcoded auth secrets leak and can't rotate
edges.example: JWT signing key committed in code
edges.resolution_rule: inject auth secrets from the secret store

edges.why_related: the ORM maps to the defined schema
edges.benefit_of_coupling: queries reflect real tables and relations
edges.risk_of_conflict: mapping an unstable schema forces rewrites
edges.example: ORM models written before the schema settles
edges.resolution_rule: stabilize the schema before building the query layer

edges.why_related: migrations realize and evolve the schema
edges.benefit_of_coupling: schema changes ship as versioned migrations
edges.risk_of_conflict: editing schema outside migrations diverges environments
edges.example: manual prod schema edit not in a migration
edges.resolution_rule: apply all schema change through migrations

edges.why_related: indexes are added on the modeled tables/columns
edges.risk_of_conflict: indexing before modeling guesses wrong
edges.example: indexes added before access patterns known
edges.resolution_rule: model first, then index for access patterns

edges.why_related: observed queries reveal which indexes are needed
edges.risk_of_conflict: indexing without query data is speculative
edges.example: adding indexes with no slow-query evidence
edges.resolution_rule: drive indexing from observed query patterns

edges.why_related: the query layer acquires connections from the pool
edges.risk_of_conflict: unpooled per-query connections exhaust the DB
edges.example: new connection opened per query
edges.resolution_rule: size the pool to the query layer's concurrency

edges.why_related: cache sits in front of expensive query-layer reads
edges.risk_of_conflict: caching before knowing hot paths wastes effort
edges.example: caching cold queries that are never reused
edges.resolution_rule: cache only measured hot read paths

edges.why_related: both reduce read latency and can mask each other's gaps
edges.risk_of_conflict: caching a slow query hides a missing index instead of fixing it
edges.example: caching around an unindexed query that should be indexed
edges.resolution_rule: fix indexing for source-of-truth speed; cache only after the query is reasonable

edges.why_related: slow lifecycle work is offloaded to background jobs
edges.risk_of_conflict: running slow work inline blocks the request
edges.example: image processing inside the HTTP handler
edges.resolution_rule: move deferrable work off the request path into a queue

edges.why_related: the proxy forwards to the managed app service
edges.benefit_of_coupling: proxy has a stable supervised upstream
edges.risk_of_conflict: proxying to an unmanaged process breaks on restart
edges.example: nginx upstream pointing at a hand-run process
edges.resolution_rule: run the app as a service before fronting it with a proxy

edges.why_related: containers receive config/secrets at runtime, not baked in
edges.benefit_of_coupling: images stay generic and secrets stay external
edges.risk_of_conflict: baking secrets into image layers leaks them
edges.example: an API key committed in a Docker layer
edges.resolution_rule: inject secrets at container runtime, never at build

edges.why_related: releases ship the built container image
edges.risk_of_conflict: deploying unbuilt or untagged images is non-reproducible
edges.example: copying source to prod instead of an image
edges.resolution_rule: build a pinned image before releasing it

edges.why_related: releases must run migrations in a compatible order
edges.risk_of_conflict: deploying code before its migration breaks runtime
edges.example: new code reads a column the migration hasn't added
edges.resolution_rule: order migrations and code deploy for compatibility

edges.why_related: release restarts/updates the managed service
edges.risk_of_conflict: deploying without service management loses restart guarantees
edges.example: manual kill-and-start with no supervision
edges.resolution_rule: drive release through the managed service

edges.why_related: the proxy/load balancer distributes traffic across instances
edges.risk_of_conflict: scaling without a balancer can't distribute load
edges.example: multiple instances with no front balancer
edges.resolution_rule: front instances with a load balancer to scale out

edges.why_related: per-instance pools multiply against the DB connection ceiling
edges.benefit_of_coupling: scaling respects total DB connection limits
edges.risk_of_conflict: scaling app instances exhausts DB connections
edges.example: 10 instances x 20 pool overrunning the DB limit
edges.resolution_rule: cap instances*pool below the database connection ceiling

edges.why_related: container images make instances identical and replaceable
edges.benefit_of_coupling: horizontal scaling clones a known image
edges.risk_of_conflict: scaling non-reproducible hosts drifts
edges.example: each scaled host configured slightly differently
edges.resolution_rule: scale from a single reproducible image

edges.why_related: service and journald provide the base signals to observe
edges.risk_of_conflict: observing an unmanaged process loses lifecycle signals
edges.example: no service logs to scrape or correlate
edges.resolution_rule: run as a service so logs/metrics have a stable source

edges.why_related: alerts and signals trigger and guide incident response
edges.risk_of_conflict: running ops without signals means blind response
edges.example: paging on a problem with no diagnostic data
edges.resolution_rule: instrument observability before relying on runbooks

edges.why_related: recovery runbooks depend on tested backups/restore
edges.benefit_of_coupling: incidents can invoke a proven restore
edges.risk_of_conflict: a restore runbook with untested backups fails
edges.example: running a restore step that has never worked
edges.resolution_rule: prove backups before writing recovery runbooks on them

edges.why_related: release health is verified through monitoring and can trigger rollback
edges.risk_of_conflict: deploying with no health signal hides regressions
edges.example: a release degrading latency unnoticed for hours
edges.resolution_rule: verify releases via monitoring; roll back on SLO breach; stop when health is green

edges.why_related: postmortems can reveal schema/data flaws to revisit
edges.risk_of_conflict: never feeding incidents back repeats failures
edges.example: the same corruption recurs with no schema fix
edges.resolution_rule: route postmortem findings to upstream nodes; stop when the action item is closed

edges.why_related: auth events are a key signal to log and alert on
edges.risk_of_conflict: unlogged auth failures hide attacks
edges.example: brute-force attempts with no auth logging
edges.resolution_rule: emit and monitor auth events for detection

edges.why_related: validation runs before authorization decisions on the parsed request
edges.risk_of_conflict: authorizing unvalidated input is error-prone
edges.example: authz on a field that was never validated
edges.resolution_rule: validate request shape before authorization logic

edges.why_related: caching responses can serve authorized data to the wrong caller
edges.risk_of_conflict: shared cache keys leak per-user authorized data
edges.example: one user seeing another's cached profile
edges.resolution_rule: never cache per-user authorized responses under shared keys; scope keys by principal

edges.why_related: queue depth and worker failures must be monitored
edges.risk_of_conflict: unmonitored queues silently back up
edges.example: a dead worker piling up jobs unnoticed
edges.resolution_rule: monitor queue depth and worker health

edges.why_related: risky releases (migrations) should be preceded by a backup
edges.risk_of_conflict: a destructive migration with no fresh backup is unrecoverable
edges.example: dropping a column with no backup to restore
edges.resolution_rule: take a verified backup before destructive releases

edges.why_related: filesystem permissions bound who can read secret files
edges.benefit_of_coupling: secrets stay readable only to the service
edges.risk_of_conflict: loose permissions expose env/secret files
edges.example: a 0644 env file readable by all users
edges.resolution_rule: restrict secret-file permissions to the service identity

edges.why_related: multiple instances need a shared cache, not per-instance state
edges.risk_of_conflict: per-instance in-memory caches diverge
edges.example: two instances showing different cached values
edges.resolution_rule: use a shared cache store when scaling horizontally

edges.why_related: scaling the app tier shifts load to the database where indexing matters
edges.risk_of_conflict: adding instances without DB tuning just saturates the DB
edges.example: quadrupling workers against an unindexed query
edges.resolution_rule: tune database/indexing before scaling the app tier into it

edges.why_related: container logs/health must be wired to monitoring
edges.risk_of_conflict: container stdout lost with no log pipeline
edges.example: container logs vanishing on restart
edges.resolution_rule: route container logs/health into the monitoring stack

edges.why_related: what to back up and the RPO follow from the data model
edges.risk_of_conflict: backing up the wrong stores misses critical data
edges.example: backing up a cache but not the primary DB
edges.resolution_rule: derive backup scope from the data model

conflict_axes.trigger: cached reads diverge from the source of truth after a write
resolution_order: invalidate on write for low-tolerance data
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: for correctness-sensitive data, freshness dominates and caching requires invalidation; for tolerant data, cache for speed
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if stale data causes user-visible incorrectness
conflict_axes.example: serving an old account balance from cache after a transaction

conflict_axes.trigger: a slow query can be indexed or simply cached
resolution_order: cache only after the source query is reasonable
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: fix the source-of-truth query via indexing before caching, so the cache does not mask a structural problem
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if a cache is hiding a query that fails on cache miss
conflict_axes.example: caching an unindexed report query that times out whenever the cache is cold

conflict_axes.trigger: strict auth/timeouts degrade legitimate user or operator experience
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: for sensitive operations security dominates; for low-risk flows minimize friction
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if a control blocks a material fraction of legitimate access
conflict_axes.example: forcing re-authentication on every request to prevent token replay

conflict_axes.trigger: adding app instances pushes more load onto a shared database
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: relieve the database bottleneck before scaling the app tier into it
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if scaling app instances saturates DB connections or CPU
conflict_axes.example: quadrupling workers while a single unindexed query saturates the DB

conflict_axes.trigger: a deadline pressures shipping without a backup or safe migration order
resolution_order: take a verified backup for destructive changes
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: for destructive or irreversible releases, safety dominates speed; reversible low-risk changes may favor speed
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if a release is irreversible without a tested rollback or backup
conflict_axes.example: running a column-drop migration to hit a date with no fresh backup

conflict_axes.trigger: a normalized schema requires expensive joins on hot read paths
resolution_order: keep the model normalized as source of truth
denormalize or cache only with a clear invariant
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: correctness via normalization dominates; controlled denormalization/caching is added only with explicit invalidation rules
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if denormalized copies drift from the source of truth
conflict_axes.example: duplicating a price into orders and forgetting to keep it in sync

conflict_axes.trigger: work is slow enough to hurt latency but the caller expects a result
resolution_order: classify work by user-visible latency need
offload deferrable work with status feedback
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: user-perceived latency dominates: defer anything not needed in the response, but expose job status
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if a deferred result is silently lost or the user has no status
conflict_axes.example: processing a large upload inline and timing out the request

conflict_axes.trigger: rich logging captures request data that may include secrets or PII
resolution_order: define what must never be logged
redact secrets/PII at the logging boundary
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: secret/PII protection dominates: redact sensitive fields even at the cost of some diagnostic detail
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if a secret or PII value reaches the log store
conflict_axes.example: an exception handler logging the full request body including an auth token

conflict_axes.trigger: an automated deploy/ops action could cause irreversible data effects
resolution_order: require human approval for irreversible/data-destructive steps
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: for irreversible or high-risk effects, human review dominates automation
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if an automated step is irreversible and lacks a tested rollback
conflict_axes.example: an auto-deploy that runs a destructive migration with no approval gate

edge_cases.trigger: an edge or dependency points at a renamed/removed node id
edge_cases.failure_mode: reference integrity breaks and the graph cannot be traversed
edge_cases.example: an edge from a node id that was renamed during editing
edge_cases.detection_method: resolve every edge from/to and dependency against the node id set
resolution: repair or remove the dangling reference

edge_cases.trigger: application code and DB schema diverge because a migration was skipped
edge_cases.example: code reading a column that the latest migration never added
edge_cases.detection_method: compare applied-migration record against expected schema on deploy
resolution: block deploy until migrations are applied

edge_cases.trigger: a heuristic estimate is treated as a measured benchmark
edge_cases.failure_mode: capacity decisions made on invented numbers
edge_cases.example: claiming a measured RPS ceiling with no load test
edge_cases.detection_method: check that no value is labeled observed/experimentally_validated without data
resolution: require a load test before quoting capacity numbers

edge_cases.trigger: a single node tries to cover build, migrate, deploy, scale, and monitor
edge_cases.failure_mode: the work unit cannot be completed or validated in one session
edge_cases.example: one 'do devops' node spanning images, releases, and scaling
edge_cases.detection_method: check each node's scope_boundary for a single coherent work unit
resolution: split the node along its scope boundary

edge_cases.trigger: a high-risk node has no acceptance tests
edge_cases.example: an auth node with no test that protected routes reject anonymous calls
edge_cases.detection_method: assert acceptance_tests non-empty for nodes with risk_if_wrong>=0.80

edge_cases.trigger: an artifact is hard-locked before validation and review gates pass
edge_cases.failure_mode: a flawed release process is frozen and hard to change
edge_cases.example: hard-locking the deploy runbook before any rollback test
edge_cases.detection_method: verify no hard_lock precedes dependency/validation/review gates

edge_cases.trigger: a failing task retries without limit or backoff
edge_cases.failure_mode: the broker floods and workers spin on a poison message
edge_cases.example: a malformed job retried forever with no dead-letter
edge_cases.detection_method: inspect retry policy for max attempts and dead-letter routing
resolution: route exhausted jobs to a dead-letter queue

edge_cases.trigger: a tradeoff between two nodes is modeled as a dependency
edge_cases.failure_mode: priority ordering and gates treat a conflict as a prerequisite
edge_cases.example: encoding cache-vs-index tension as a dependency edge
edge_cases.detection_method: check conflict tensions are conflict edges with signed_tension<0, not dependencies

edge_cases.trigger: a dependent node is prioritized before its prerequisite
edge_cases.failure_mode: work starts on a node whose inputs are not ready
edge_cases.example: ordering auth before the request lifecycle it plugs into

edge_cases.trigger: a guideline or default referenced is outdated for the current stack
edge_cases.example: following a deprecated secret-handling pattern for the framework

edge_cases.trigger: a workflow step ends without its required handoff artifact
edge_cases.failure_mode: the next session/operator lacks the context to proceed
edge_cases.example: a deploy step that produces no rollback record
edge_cases.detection_method: assert each major workflow step emits its handoff artifact contents
resolution: block exit until handoff is complete

edge_cases.trigger: a computed score is inconsistent with its formula or label
edge_cases.failure_mode: priority and risk reasoning use wrong numbers
edge_cases.example: a final_importance that does not match the node formula
edge_cases.detection_method: recompute all derived fields and compare within tolerance 0.02
resolution: recompute derived fields from base metrics

workflow.objective: define the API contract and resource model
acceptance_tests: every endpoint has a documented schema
versioning policy defined
workflow.do_first_because: every downstream layer inherits the API contract

workflow.objective: design the relational data model and constraints
acceptance_tests: key relationships have foreign-key constraints
schema supports primary access patterns
workflow.do_first_because: the data model is a high-irreversibility foundation for the data layer

workflow.objective: wire the request lifecycle, validation, and auth
acceptance_tests: protected routes reject anonymous access
invalid input is rejected at the boundary
workflow.do_first_because: auth and validation are high-risk controls that gate all request handling

workflow.objective: build the query layer, migrations, and performance basics
acceptance_tests: each migration has a rollback or forward-fix
hot queries meet a latency baseline
workflow.do_first_because: migrations and access patterns must be stable before deploy couples to them

workflow.objective: offload deferrable work to background jobs
acceptance_tests: retried tasks are idempotent
exhausted jobs go to a dead-letter queue
workflow.do_first_because: queues must be defined before deploy and monitoring wrap them

workflow.objective: run the app as a managed service with secure access and secrets
acceptance_tests: the service auto-restarts on crash and boot
no secret is committed or world-readable
workflow.do_first_because: a secure managed host is the foundation the proxy, deploy, and ops build on

workflow.objective: front the service with a reverse proxy and TLS
acceptance_tests: TLS terminates correctly at the proxy
upstream routing and timeouts are correct
workflow.do_first_because: the proxy must front a managed service before traffic is exposed or scaled

workflow.objective: package the app and release it with migrations and rollback
acceptance_tests: a failed release rolls back without data loss
migrations and code deploy in a compatible order
exit_criteria: release process reviewed and rollback tested
workflow.do_first_because: release is irreversible-prone and must follow stable migrations and host config

workflow.objective: scale horizontally behind a load balancer
acceptance_tests: any instance can serve any request
instances*pool stays under the DB connection ceiling
workflow.do_first_because: scaling depends on a stateless app and a fronting load balancer

workflow.objective: observe, back up, and operate the running system
acceptance_tests: alerts fire before users report outages
a backup restores within the RTO
common failures have runbooks
workflow.do_first_because: operability and recoverability are verified last and gate the hard lock

dominance_rules.trigger: a high-risk change conflicts with a deadline
dominance_rules.rule: remediating high-risk issues dominates schedule pressure
dominance_rules.required_action: fix, retest, or formally accept high-risk items before shipping
dominance_rules.example: shipping an open data-loss risk to hit a date

dominance_rules.trigger: a high-value node has unmet prerequisites
dominance_rules.required_action: schedule prerequisites before dependents regardless of value
dominance_rules.example: building scaling before the app is stateless

dominance_rules.trigger: a number looks precise but lacks measured data
dominance_rules.example: quoting a benchmark RPS with no load test

dominance_rules.trigger: an artifact is about to be locked before tests pass
dominance_rules.required_action: do not lock until acceptance tests and gates pass
dominance_rules.example: hard-locking the release before a rollback test

dominance_rules.trigger: an automated action is irreversible or data-destructive
dominance_rules.rule: human review dominates automation for irreversible effects
dominance_rules.required_action: require approval and a decision record before irreversible actions

dominance_rules.trigger: schema stability conflicts with adding more objects
dominance_rules.rule: schema consistency dominates raw object count
dominance_rules.example: adding nodes that duplicate existing concepts

dominance_rules.trigger: cached data may be served stale for correctness-sensitive reads
dominance_rules.rule: correctness dominates cache speed for sensitive data
dominance_rules.required_action: invalidate on write or bypass cache for sensitive reads
dominance_rules.example: serving a stale balance from cache after a transaction

dominance_rules.trigger: a security control degrades legitimate access
dominance_rules.rule: for sensitive operations security dominates convenience
dominance_rules.required_action: apply risk-based controls scaled to data sensitivity
dominance_rules.example: disabling auth to make an integration easier

dominance_rules.trigger: a claim exceeds what the source supports
dominance_rules.required_action: downgrade or remove claims beyond the source scope
dominance_rules.example: asserting measured uptime with no measurement

dominance_rules.trigger: a locally optimal step would force later rework
dominance_rules.required_action: sequence to stabilize foundations before dependents
dominance_rules.example: tuning indexes before the schema is settled

anti_rework_rules.rule: fix the API contract before building lifecycle, validation, and data access
anti_rework_rules.rationale: layers built on an unstable contract are reworked on every change
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: a handler or schema changes whenever the contract shifts
anti_rework_rules.example: writing validation models before endpoints are decided

anti_rework_rules.rule: stabilize the data model before the ORM, indexes, and migrations depend on it
anti_rework_rules.rationale: query layer and indexes built on a shifting schema are rewritten
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: ORM models or indexes change every time the schema does
anti_rework_rules.example: indexing columns before access patterns are known

anti_rework_rules.rule: provision secret management before wiring auth and containers
anti_rework_rules.rationale: auth built on hardcoded secrets must be reworked to rotate them
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: auth keys appear in code or image layers
anti_rework_rules.example: committing a JWT signing key to the repo

anti_rework_rules.rule: validate request shape before authorization logic reasons over it
anti_rework_rules.rationale: authz over unvalidated input is fragile and reworked
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: authz reads a field that was never validated
anti_rework_rules.example: granting access based on an unparsed client value

anti_rework_rules.rule: run the app as a managed service before fronting it with a proxy
anti_rework_rules.rationale: a proxy in front of an unmanaged process breaks on restart
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: upstream errors after a manual process dies
anti_rework_rules.example: pointing nginx at a hand-run process

anti_rework_rules.rule: make migrations reversible and ordered before coupling deploy to them
blocked_until: migrations have tested rollback or forward-fix
anti_rework_rules.rationale: a deploy coupled to bad migrations breaks mid-release
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: a release fails because code precedes its migration
anti_rework_rules.example: deploying code that reads a not-yet-added column

anti_rework_rules.rule: build a reproducible image before releasing it
anti_rework_rules.rationale: releasing non-reproducible artifacts is reworked per environment
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: each environment runs a slightly different build
anti_rework_rules.example: copying source to prod instead of an image

anti_rework_rules.rule: tune database performance before scaling the app tier into it
blocked_until: hot queries meet a baseline and pool math is sized
anti_rework_rules.rationale: scaling onto an unindexed DB just saturates it and is rolled back
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: added instances do not improve throughput
anti_rework_rules.example: quadrupling workers against an unindexed query

anti_rework_rules.rule: take a verified backup before destructive or irreversible releases
anti_rework_rules.rationale: a destructive change with no backup is unrecoverable rework
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: a dropped column cannot be recovered
anti_rework_rules.example: running a column-drop with no fresh backup

anti_rework_rules.rule: instrument observability before relying on incident runbooks
blocked_until: logging, metrics, and alerts in place
anti_rework_rules.rationale: running ops blind forces guesswork and repeated incidents
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: incidents are detected by users, not alerts
anti_rework_rules.example: paging on an issue with no diagnostic signal

iteration_protocol.trigger: a validator, test, or monitor reports a failure
acceptance_tests: every failure mapped to a subsystem

iteration_protocol.detection: rank defects by risk_score and irreversibility
acceptance_tests: highest-risk defect is first
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: queue is empty or only sub-threshold defects remain

iteration_protocol.trigger: a defect touches a high-coupling node
iteration_protocol.detection: trace edges and dependents from the defect node
acceptance_tests: all dependents of the defect are listed
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: impact set is stable across a pass

iteration_protocol.trigger: a defect is selected for repair
iteration_protocol.detection: map the defect type to a repair subsystem
acceptance_tests: the defect's repair owner is recorded

iteration_protocol.trigger: a repair changed a node, edge, or score
iteration_protocol.detection: re-run the validator over the changed artifact
acceptance_tests: the repaired check now passes

iteration_protocol.trigger: new information would change a node's importance
iteration_protocol.detection: compare new posterior to prior beyond the revisit delta
acceptance_tests: posterior change beyond delta is recorded
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: no node moves beyond the revisit delta

iteration_protocol.trigger: a defect is irreversible or high-risk and unresolved
iteration_protocol.detection: check risk_if_wrong and irreversibility against thresholds
acceptance_tests: the irreversible defect has a human decision record
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: no unresolved high-risk irreversible defect remains

iteration_protocol.trigger: a new KB version is produced
iteration_protocol.detection: compare counts and scores against the prior version
acceptance_tests: no required check regressed
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: no regressions remain or each is accepted with a record
